text:
Help me write a case for my promotion. I'm the assistant front office manager at a 180-room hotel, and the front office manager job is open. I'm applying, and my general manager wants it in writing by Friday.

Facts:
- I've worked here 6 years, the last 2 as assistant manager.
- Our guest score for check-in on the main review site went from 7.9 to 8.6 over the last 18 months. The lobby and all the rooms were renovated during the same time.
- I rewrote the front desk training. New hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9.
- Front desk turnover was 9 of 14 people in the year before I became assistant manager, and 5 of 14 last year.
- I've covered the front office manager's job alone for the 7 weeks since she left.
- I have never managed a budget. The front office manager owns a $1.1 million payroll budget.

I want it to say I'm the main reason our guest scores went up. One page.

Before I draft, a few questions. Your answers will change what the page says.

One thing first. Your GM saw the lobby and every room get renovated during the same 18 months the score went up. If the page says you're the main reason, they'll probably think of the renovation straight away, and that doubt can spill over onto your other numbers, which are strong. A safer claim is that you drove the front desk's part of the improvement, backed by evidence that separates staff from the new rooms. Question 1 is about finding that evidence.

1. **Do you have anything that links the score rise to the front desk rather than the renovation?** For example: when the new training started compared with when the renovation finished; whether the score rose before the renovation was done; a separate staff or service sub-score; or reviews that praise check-in staff, especially by name.
2. **What did you change that you think cut turnover from 9 of 14 to 5 of 14?** Scheduling, onboarding, recognition, how you handle problems? The GM will want to know whether it's repeatable.
3. **What can you show from the 7 weeks you've covered the job alone?** Did scores, overtime, staffing or complaints hold steady or improve? Did you handle anything hard, like a big group, a staffing gap or an escalation?
4. **Have you done anything close to budget work?** Building schedules against forecast occupancy, controlling overtime, approving hours, labor reports? And would you sign up for something specific to learn the $1.1M payroll budget, like working alongside the controller or a course? I'd rather say this openly than leave it out, because your GM already knows it's the gap.
5. **What does your GM care about most right now?** Labor cost, review scores, staff retention, something else? That decides what goes first.

If you don't know an answer, just say so. I'll leave that point out rather than guess.

1. The renovation started 5 months into those 18 months, and check-in had already gone from 7.9 to 8.2 before it started. I don't know when the new training started compared to the renovation, and I don't know about a staff sub-score or reviews naming people. I'm fine dropping "main reason" and just saying what I did.

2. I don't know.

3. In the 7 weeks, no front desk shift went uncovered and overtime came in under the monthly plan. Complaints about check-in waits on Friday evenings are still the most common complaint at the desk. I don't know about scores in that stretch or anything specific I handled.

4. Only the overtime coming in under plan during the 7 weeks. I can commit to finishing the company's finance course in my first 3 months (company pays), and to weekly sessions on the payroll budget with our controller, Ben Oduya. He's already offered.

5. I don't know.

I left out "main reason" and wrote only what you did. The page says the score had already risen from 7.9 to 8.2 before the renovation began. It doesn't say your training caused that, because you don't know when the training started. Your GM can draw the conclusion.

<final_document>
**To:** [General Manager's name]
**From:** [Your name], Assistant Front Office Manager
**Date:** [Date]
**Re:** My application for Front Office Manager

I'm applying for the Front Office Manager position. I've done this job on my own for the past seven weeks, and I'd like to keep doing it. Below is what I've delivered, the one gap I have, and how I'll close it.

**The last seven weeks**
Since [previous FOM's name] left, I've run the front office alone. In that time, no front desk shift has gone uncovered and overtime has come in under the monthly plan.

**Two years as Assistant Front Office Manager**

- **Faster training.** I rewrote our front desk training. New hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9, which saves four shifts of shadowing for every person we hire.
- **Lower turnover.** In the year before I became assistant manager, 9 of our 14 front desk staff left. Last year, 5 of 14 left.
- **Higher check-in scores.** Our check-in score on [review site] rose from 7.9 to 8.6 over the past 18 months. The renovation clearly helped. However, the score had already reached 8.2 before renovation work started, so part of the gain came before any guest saw a new room or the new lobby.

I've worked at this hotel for six years. I know the team, the systems and our guests, and you won't need to wait for me to learn the property.

**My gap: budget ownership**
I have never managed a budget, and this role owns a $1.1 million payroll budget. The closest I've come is keeping overtime under plan these past seven weeks. To close the gap, I commit to:

- Finishing the company's finance course within my first three months.
- Meeting weekly with Ben Oduya, our controller, to work through the payroll budget. He has already offered to do this.

**My first priority**
Friday evening check-in waits are still the most common complaint at our desk. Fixing them would be my first focus as Front Office Manager.

I'd welcome the chance to talk this through before you decide. Thank you for considering me.
</final_document>

Before you send it:

- **Friday waits:** You told me about the complaint but not what you'd do about it, so I named it as your first priority without a plan. If you have an idea, such as adding Friday evening staff or offering online check-in, add one sentence. If you'd rather not raise it, delete that section.
- **Placeholders:** Fill in the names, the date and the review site.
- **Turnover:** I listed the numbers without explaining why turnover fell, because you weren't sure. If your GM asks, it's fine to say you're still working out which changes made the difference.
